chat.author: Felix Linker

chat.author: Andrew Campling
chat.text: Not disagreeing with Lars-Johan, but I note that there are some pretty exotic uses of the DNS out there.  For example, an implementation of Doom on the DNS. (Not suggesting that is a good idea!)

chat.author: Felix Linker
chat.text:
Andrew Campling said:

Not disagreeing with Lars-Johan, but I note that there are some pretty exotic uses of the DNS out there.  For example, an implementation of Doom on the DNS. (Not suggesting that is a good idea!)

Are DNAME records the instructions?

chat.author: Felix Linker
chat.text: Ah, no. DNS is not Turing complete, I believe. Anyway...

chat.author: Andrew Campling
chat.text: "The idea behind DOOM on DNS is to use DNS TXT records—fields originally intended for text like email authentication—to store arbitrary data, including the game's code and assets. Each TXT record can hold about 2,000 characters, and a DNS zone can contain thousands of records. By splitting the DOOM game files into chunks and encoding them in Base64, the game can be transmitted and reassembled entirely through DNS queries, without ever writing files to disk"

chat.author: Jim Reid
chat.text: Take a look at NATPR records Felix. These are Turing-complete IMO.

chat.author: Jim Reid
chat.text: As Liman said a few minutes ago, DNS is bad for holding big chunks of data. So store these elsewhere and put a pointer to that location in the DNS.

chat.author: Jim Reid

chat.author: Orie Steele
chat.text:
Not sure selective disclosure is needed for this...
IMO, just need to put emblem in DNS, point it at stuff that is meant to be covered by it.
and pull extra data from remote resources if you need more details on the specific emblem, or put selective disclosure structures in these remote resources.

chat.author: Alex Rosenberg
chat.text: For me the important part is that the domain holder is the one asserting these facts and that chain of trust is rooted by DNSSEC and not a trust store of subvertable keys. I'd strongly suggest that pointers to non-DNS spots be pinned via something like DANE.

chat.author: Rohan Mahy
chat.text:
Regarding selective disclosure, we have heard three overall approaches:

DNS as an application server
encrypted information in DNS and the relevant key distribution
DNS points to an application-leyer protocol
I think we can task the proponents to provide an existence proof of how to implement each of the three options and compare their properties.

chat.author: Martin Thomson
chat.text: The slide is helpful, but what I would generally expect to see from an architecture is a set of roles and how those roles plan to interact.  The architecture would address incentives and threat models.  This notion of profiles is also an architectural concept that might be there.

chat.author: Martin Thomson

chat.author: Orie Steele

chat.author: Alex Rosenberg
chat.text: @Martin my view is "flows and responsibilities" -- I think of an arch doc as an overview of what protocol docs will follow, but it needs to be a living document that changes as we learn during the protocol phase.

chat.author: Martin Thomson
chat.text: I'm not a fan of flows, because they tend to obscure the objectives of each actor.  I didn't have a formal reference for this until yesterday, but I was pointed at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Promise_theory and that seems a useful way to think about things.

chat.author: Martin Thomson
chat.text: It can be helpful to show an overview that includes flows, but doing so exclusively is both hard to follow and it best suited to systems with centralized control, not those where interoperability plays a key role.
